--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.trophic_levels()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Calculate the trophic level of every node in a directed graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.trophic_levels()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Calculate the trophic level of every node in a directed graph. title: >- [Graph.trophic_levels()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Calculate the trophic level of every node in a directed graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the trophic level of every node in a directed graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L62387-L62513){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.trophic_levels( weighted=None, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Trophic levels](../assets/graphs/trophic-levels.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A food web drawn left to right by trophic level: grass G feeds rabbit R and mouse M, both feed fox F, and mouse and fox feed owl O. Grass is basal at level 1, the rabbit and mouse sit at 2, the fox at 3, and the owl, eating at levels 2 and 3, at 3.5, the top of the table." width="100%"} Trophic levels come from food-web ecology (Levine, 1980), where an edge points from prey to predator. Basal nodes, those with no incoming edges (plants), have level 1, and every other node sits one level above the average level of what feeds it, weighted by edge weight. The result is a continuous hierarchy: a node fed half by plants (level 1) and half by herbivores (level 2) gets level 2.5. The same idea measures position in any flow or dependency network: citation chains, supply chains, or the layering of a software system. Every node must be reachable from a basal node, or levels are undefined. Edge weights are used on a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`), unless `weighted=` says otherwise. Self-loops (cannibalism) count toward a node's diet. See also `trophic_differences()` and `trophic_incoherence_parameter()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to weight diets by edge weight. If `None` (default), follows the graph. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store levels in. If `None` (default), uses `"trophic_levels"`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores the levels as a node attribute and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping node IDs to levels (basal nodes are `1.0`). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected, has no basal node, or has a node not reachable from one. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~trophic_differences`) : The level difference across each edge. [](`~trophic_incoherence_parameter`) : How far the graph is from a perfect hierarchy. [](`~topological_sort`) : An order of a DAG with no levels. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this small food web, the fox eats rabbits and mice (both at level 2), so it sits at level 3. The owl eats mice (2) and foxes (3), so it sits at `1 + (2 + 3) / 2 = 3.5`: ::: {#b0425622 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec web = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("grass", "rabbit"), ("grass", "mouse"), ("rabbit", "fox"), ("mouse", "fox"), ("mouse", "owl"), ("fox", "owl")], directed=True, ) web.trophic_levels().get_node_df().select("label", "trophic_levels") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Layers of prerequisites In `courses()`, each edge points from a prerequisite to a course that requires it, so a course's trophic level is one more than the average level of its prerequisites. Most of the 200-level courses sit at level 3, but Probability and Statistics (STAT201) is at 4, level with the 300-level courses: it comes at the end of a chain of three math courses: ::: {#989683f8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl courses = ( ec.courses() .trophic_levels() .layout_multipartite(subset_key="level") ) ( courses.get_node_df() .filter(pl.col("level") == 200) .select("label", "title", "trophic_levels") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Levels in a food web `food_web()` is a made-up woodland food web, with an edge from each food to each species that eats it. The plants are at level 1 and the animals that eat only plants at level 2. The Fox eats frogs and shrews (level 3) and rabbits (level 2), so it sits at 3.67, above the Hawk at 3.5: ::: {#38953e14 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} web = ec.food_web().trophic_levels() ( web.get_node_df() .select("label", "kind", "trophic_levels") .sort("trophic_levels", descending=True) .head(5) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
